extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of natural philosophy, mechanics, and physiology (non-expert to mathematically literate)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing muscle force via pulley models
extracted.subtask_description: Use mechanical (pulley/lever) analogies and simple trigonometric factors to compute the force and velocity properties of muscle fibres and whole muscles, and to reason about how fibre number, geometry, and supports affect stresses and motion. Focus is on deriving aggregate force from single-unit elements and on the role of geometry/attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition principle — additive contributions of small machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Each small 'machine' (elementary unit within a fibre) exerts a proper force and bears a respective part; when many such small machines are united they accumulate their powers and mutually assist to raise a weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout (e.g., §94–96). Model a fibre as many little pulley-like machines; compute aggregate force by summing identical unit contributions. Example: many identical units each exerting X produce total ≈ N·X. Anti-pattern: treating units as non-interacting when they are mechanically coupled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium invariance under multiplication of machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the number of little machines may be increased, the joined system will not be able to raise or poise in equilibrium a greater weight than a single appropriate comparator weight T; multiplying units does not increase the equilibrium weight that can be held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated explicitly (§101). Multiplication of units increases capacity to change velocity (see separate criterion) but does not change the maximum static equilibrium weight caused by the same driving force. Example: adding more pulleys increases speed but not the maximal weight held in equilibrium by a given driving weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity multiplication by adding machines/pulleys
rubrics_metrics.description: By increasing the number of pulleys/little machines, the velocity with which the suspended weight rises is proportionally augmented — more units yield greater velocity of the load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in §101 and illustrated in §98–100 and §102. Quantitative relation: as number of little machines is multiplied, the height (and thus speed) through which the main weight rises in a given time increases in proportion. Example: doubling number of machines may double rise distance per unit time (with the same driving action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute fibre/muscle force by scaling single-unit force
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute the force of a carnous fibre or a whole muscle, multiply the force of one elementary machine/unit by the number of such machines composing the fibre/muscle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given in §104–108 and used in numeric examples (§108–116, §131–136). Example: if one little machine exerts 223 lb and a fibre contains 40 such machines, the fibre exerts 40·223 = 8920 lb; multiply further by number of fibres/sides to get whole-muscle force. Caution: account for later doubling due to fixed attachments and geometric factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed support (nail) contributes equivalent strain — doubling effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A cord fastened to an immovable support (a nail) sustains as great a strain as if it bore an equal weight at the other end; when one end of a muscle/tendon is fixed, the effective force/strain can be equivalent to having an equal opposing weight, effectively doubling contributions in some calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in §111–116 and applied to double forces when a muscle is fixed at one end (§135–136). Use this to justify doubling earlier computed forces for muscles attached immovably at one tendon. Example: compute single-end tension and then double to account for fixed-anchor equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obliquity (angle) increases required pull by secant factor
rubrics_metrics.description: When fibres/tendons act obliquely to the line of action, the force a fibre must exert is increased by a geometric factor related to the secant (or cosine) of the obliquity angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in §122–130 using trigonometric tables: as angle of obliquity increases, required tensile force scales approximately as secant(angle). Example: for 45° obliquity, factor ≈ 1.414; for small angles (8°) secant ≈ 1.00952 so force increases slightly. Guidance: use sine/secant tables or ratio computations (as in the text) to convert angle to multiplicative force factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-fibre load decreases with fibre number; total remains same
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing the muscle's total force among many fibres reduces the load each fibre bears, but the total capacity of the muscle (as computed from single-unit contributions and geometry) remains the same regardless of whether force is pictured as concentrated in a few fibres or spread among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in §140–151 and §154–156. Practical implication: increasing the assumed number of fibres reduces per-fibre stress (good for preventing damage) but does not change the total muscle force calculated from the model. Example: if 446 lb is total for a muscle, 2 fibres would each bear ~223 lb while 1000 fibres each bear ~0.446 lb (pro rata).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplifying geometric models permissible if aggregate properties preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing complex, three-dimensional, pyramidal or 'verticillated' fibre distributions as simple planar 'sides' does not alter the computed total force so long as aggregate geometry and unit counts are preserved; the simplification is admissible for conveying demonstrations to non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument given in §139–141 and §150–153. Use planar approximations to ease calculation but justify by showing equivalence (e.g., via distribution arguments or by equivalent summation of unit contributions). Anti-pattern: assuming planar model changes aggregate force without checking equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity augmentation requires increased force even at constant load
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase the velocity of a given load a driving mechanism must supply additional force (or additional equivalent weights); thus multiplying units to increase speed demands extra force input even if the load mass is unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained and exemplified in §159–160 and illustrated with balance/steelyard example (§160). Example: moving a weight along a longer arc in the same time (so higher speed) requires proportionally more driving force; remedy by adding weights (E, F) to maintain balance at higher speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lever-arm (length) ratios to compute tendon/muscle moment and required force
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute required tendon/muscle force by comparing lever-arm lengths: force needed to produce equilibrium equals (distance ratio)·(opposing weight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in §119–123: e.g., if tendon must be raised to X and lever arm lengths relate as 31 semidiameters etc., then multiply weight by lever ratio to get required tendon force. Apply basic lever/torque relations; be mindful of oblique geometries which further modify the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulley/weight analogies for muscle modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Model muscle fibres and their composite action using pulley-and-weight machines: cords, pulleys, nails (fixed points), and suspended weights stand as analogues of tendons, joints, fixed attachments, and loads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire demonstration (§93–103, §141–149) uses pulley analogies (Borelli's method). Guidance: map biological elements to mechanical analogs consistently (movable ends ≈ moving fibre ends, nails ≈ fixed tendons, small machines ≈ elementary contractile units). This helps compute aggregate forces and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical scaling practice — multiply unit force by counts then adjust for geometry/supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical calculation method: (1) determine unit force (force per elementary machine), (2) multiply by number of units per fibre and number of fibres/sides, (3) adjust for obliquity (secant factors) and for fixed-anchor doubling as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow worked examples (§108–116, §129–136, §131–136, §154). Example pipeline: unit=223 lb → fiber of 40 units = 8920 lb → four sides = 35680 lb → account for fixed tendon doubling to reach final reported numbers. Keep numeric rounding and significant-figure caveats in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate per-unit stress to assess tissue safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the stress borne by each elementary machine/fibre: with large numbers of units the stress per unit is very small (example: ≲ 2.5 ounces per machine in the author's computation), which explains why delicate fibres are not torn under total loads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reassure plausibility (§156–158). Compute total load divided by total unit count to obtain per-unit load. Use this to evaluate whether tendon/fibre tensile strength required is physiologically plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute contributions of many oblique small forces by fractioning total weight and applying geometric ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When many small weights/forces act obliquely, each contributes a fraction (e.g., 1/1000th) of the total perpendicular load; to find the actual tensile requirement per small weight, divide the perpendicular share by the cosine factor (i.e., multiply by secant ratio of the oblique angle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in §141–147. Example: total D = 442 lb, 1000 small weights ⇒ each must supply 1/1000 of D perpendicular; because each pulls obliquely at 8°, actual required gravity for each small weight is elevated by ratio GM/GN (≈ secant(8°)). Use trigonometric conversion to compute final per-weight requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-check — verify limiting behavior (many fibres vs. few)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that increasing the assumed number of fibres to very large values tends to reduce per-fibre loads while leaving total force unchanged — this is a consistency test for the chosen model and computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested in §150–156 and §154. Practical test: recompute totals assuming 2, 1000, or 100000 fibres and verify total remains same; inconsistencies indicate modelling or arithmetic errors.
